title: Capstone Planning: Model Inventory and Products
learningObjectives: Translate shop inventory requirements into relational entities.
Create category and product tables with primary and foreign keys.
Use UNIQUE, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints for domain rules.
Explain the one-to-many relationship between categories and products.
Query products with their category names using a join.

understand.concept: A database capstone starts with requirements and a relational model. For an inventory and sales application, categories and products are separate entities connected by a foreign key. Product price and stock quantity need domain rules.
understand.whyItMatters: A clear data model prevents duplicate category text, inconsistent prices and disconnected inventory records.
understand.analogy: A database capstone is like a complete shop workflow: records, rules, operations and reports must all work together.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model database isolation, concurrent workloads, deployment security or recovery guarantees.

explain.narrative:
## Capstone scenario
Build a small inventory and sales database for a shop. The system must store product categories, products, customers, orders and order items. It must report sales and protect stock data.

## Model the entities
A category can contain many products. Each product belongs to one category. Give each entity a primary key and use a foreign key for the relationship.

## Domain rules
Product names should be required, prices and stock quantities should not be negative, and category names should be unique. Use database constraints for rules that must hold regardless of which application writes the data.

### Model review
The category-to-product relationship is one-to-many: one category can classify multiple products, while each product row references one category. A production model should also define whether product names or codes are unique, how discontinued products are represented, and whether price changes require an audit history.

### SQLite integrity setting
Enable and verify `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` on every SQLite connection used for the exercise. Test an invalid category_id to prove the runtime is enforcing the relationship.

examples.title: Create product categories
examples.code: CREATE TABLE cap19_categories (category_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
examples.explanation: Creates a category lookup table. category_id is the stable key used by other tables, while UNIQUE on category_name prevents two categories from sharing the same name. In SQLite, INTEGER PRIMARY KEY aliases the rowid.

examples.title: Create products with a category relationship
examples.code: CREATE TABLE cap19_products (product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES cap19_categories(category_id), product_name TEXT NOT NULL, unit_price REAL NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0), stock_qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (stock_qty >= 0));
examples.explanation: Creates products and references categories with a foreign key. CHECK constraints reject negative prices and stock quantities. SQLite foreign-key enforcement must be enabled for each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; declaring REFERENCES alone does not guarantee enforcement in every SQLite connection.

examples.title: Insert categories
examples.explanation: Inserts the two category parent rows first. Parent records must exist before child product rows are inserted when foreign-key enforcement is active.

examples.title: Insert products
examples.code: INSERT INTO cap19_products VALUES (1, 1, 'USB Cable', 250, 20), (2, 1, 'Phone Case', 400, 12), (3, 2, 'Notebook', 60, 50);
examples.explanation: Inserts three products and links each one to an existing category ID. The numeric values are valid under the CHECK constraints. REAL is used for a compact teaching example; production currency should use an exact decimal type where available or integer minor units to avoid binary floating-point rounding.

examples.title: List products with their category
examples.code: SELECT p.product_name, c.category_name, p.unit_price, p.stock_qty FROM cap19_products AS p JOIN cap19_categories AS c ON c.category_id = p.category_id ORDER BY p.product_id;
examples.expectedOutput: USB Cable | Accessories | 250.0 | 20; Phone Case | Accessories | 400.0 | 12; Notebook | Stationery | 60.0 | 50
examples.explanation: Joins products to categories through category_id rather than matching category names. The selected columns combine product attributes with the category label, and ORDER BY product_id makes the displayed row sequence deterministic.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and inspect the category-product relationship. Identify which constraints prevent duplicate categories and negative stock.
practise.independentTask: Extend the model with suppliers. Design a supplier table and connect products to suppliers using a foreign key; explain the relationship cardinality.
hints: Separate categories and products into different tables.
Use a primary key for each entity.
Use a foreign key from products to categories.
Use CHECK constraints for non-negative price and stock.
Join the tables to display category names with products.

questions.prompt: Why store categories in a separate table?
options: To avoid repeating category data and to enforce a relationship
To make every product have two prices
questions.answer: To avoid repeating category data and to enforce a relationship
questions.explanation: A separate category entity avoids repeated text and supports referential integrity.

questions.prompt: Which constraint prevents duplicate category names?
questions.explanation: UNIQUE prevents duplicate values in the category_name column.

questions.prompt: What does the product category_id foreign key enforce?
options: Each referenced category must exist when foreign keys are enforced
Every category must have one product
questions.answer: Each referenced category must exist when foreign keys are enforced
questions.explanation: The foreign key links a product to an existing category.
CHECK enforces the allowed price domain.

questions.prompt: Which join displays category names with product rows?
options: JOIN products to categories on category_id
questions.answer: JOIN products to categories on category_id
questions.explanation: A join matches each product's category_id to the category primary key.
